title: Le Tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours
author: Jules Verne
blurb: A bet at a London club, a French valet, a detective in pursuit, an elephant across India, a ship burned plank by plank, and one day that nobody counted.

p: In 1872, the house at number 7 Savile Row, in London, was lived in by Phileas Fogg, one of the most remarkable members of the Reform Club.
He was a rich, calm and silent man, whose past nobody knew.
His life ran like clockwork: he got up at the same time, lunched at the club at the same table, read the same newspapers, and played cards every evening with the same friends.
He had never left London, but he knew the map of the world better than anyone.
On 2 October, at the club, people were talking about a daring theft: a thief had taken fifty-five thousand pounds from the Bank of England, and he had vanished.
'He won't be able to hide for long,' said one of the players. 'The earth has become too small. Nowadays you can go round it in three months.'
'In only eighty days,' replied Phileas Fogg calmly.
His friends burst out laughing. On paper, perhaps; but a storm, a late train, a missed boat would be enough for everything to fail.
'I bet twenty thousand pounds that I will go round the world in eighty days,' said Fogg. 'I leave tonight.'
The bet was accepted. If Fogg was back at the Reform Club before Saturday 21 December at a quarter to nine in the evening, he would have won. If not, he would be ruined.
That very morning, Fogg had hired a new servant, a Frenchman of about thirty, called Passepartout.
Passepartout had had an eventful life: he had been a singer, a circus acrobat and a fireman, and he was at last looking for a quiet master.
When Fogg told him they were leaving on a journey round the world in ten minutes, he first thought it was a joke.
They took a single bag, in which Fogg put twenty thousand pounds in banknotes.
Seven days later, at Suez, a nervous little man was watching the passengers getting off the steamer.
His name was Fix, and he was a police inspector.
When he saw Phileas Fogg, he was certain he had found the Bank of England thief: a rich gentleman fleeing London with a bag full of banknotes, who else could it be?
Unfortunately, he had not yet received the warrant that would allow him to arrest him.
So he decided to follow him, from one country to the next, until the warrant arrived.
In Bombay, Fogg and Passepartout took the train that crosses India to Calcutta.
But in the middle of the forest, the train stopped abruptly. The driver announced that the line was not finished: fifty miles of rails were missing.
The newspapers had announced the opening of the line a little too soon.
The other travellers complained; Fogg, for his part, did not lose his calm.
He found a villager who owned an elephant, and he bought it from him for two thousand pounds, an enormous sum.
With a young guide and an English officer, Sir Francis Cromarty, who was going in the same direction, they set off through the forest, perched on the animal's back.
Passepartout, shaken in all directions, was laughing like a child. Never had he travelled in such an extraordinary way.
On the second day, they heard chanting in the forest and saw a long procession pass by.
In the middle, priests were leading a young woman dressed in silk and covered in jewellery, who seemed barely conscious.
The guide explained to them that her name was Aouda, that she was the widow of an old prince, and that she was to die the next day on her husband's funeral pyre, according to an ancient custom.
She had been drugged so that she would not resist.
'We still have twelve hours in hand,' said Fogg. 'I can devote them to saving her.'
Sir Francis looked at him in surprise. So this cold man had a heart.
During the night, they tried to get close to the temple, but it was guarded on every side.
At dawn, the crowd gathered around the pyre. Fogg was about to rush forward, alone against everyone, when something unexpected happened.
The dead old prince seemed to rise, took the young woman in his arms, and came down from the pyre in the middle of the smoke.
Terrified, the priests and the crowd threw themselves face down on the ground.
It was Passepartout! Taking advantage of the darkness, he had slipped onto the pyre and taken the dead man's place.
A few minutes later, the elephant was carrying them all off into the forest, with Aouda, saved.
Aouda, who had been brought up in India in an English family, spoke perfect English. Fogg offered to take her as far as Hong Kong, where one of her relatives lived.
But in Hong Kong, they learned that this relative had left the city. Fogg then simply said to her: 'Come to Europe with us.'
Fix, meanwhile, was in despair. His warrant still hadn't arrived, and Hong Kong was the last English territory before America.
Fogg absolutely had to stay there.
He invited Passepartout to a tavern, made him drink until he fell asleep, and the servant was unable to warn his master that the boat for Japan was leaving that same evening, earlier than planned.
Passepartout woke up just in time to get on the boat, alone. Fogg and Aouda had stayed ashore.
Arriving in Yokohama without a penny, he had to look for work, and he got himself hired by a troupe of Japanese acrobats, the 'Long Noses'.
During the show, he was forming the base of a human pyramid when he caught sight of Phileas Fogg and Aouda in the front row.
He leapt towards them, and the whole pyramid collapsed amid the shouts of the audience.
Fogg, without wasting a moment, had hired a little boat to reach Japan. He paid the circus manager, and they left for San Francisco.
From San Francisco to New York, they had to cross America by train: seven days' travel, through deserts, mountains and the great plains.
Fix had followed them. He now had his warrant, but he could only use it on English territory.
So he decided to help Fogg get back to England as quickly as possible, so as to arrest him there.
The journey was full of adventures.
One day, a herd of bison crossed the track, and the train had to wait three hours for them to pass.
Another day, they had to cross at full speed a bridge that was threatening to collapse: it fell into the river just after the last carriage had passed.

Later still, the train was attacked, and Passepartout, who had managed to save it by uncoupling the locomotive, was taken prisoner. Fogg did not hesitate for a second to go and free him, at the risk of missing the next train.
He did miss it. To reach Omaha, they had to cross the frozen plain on a sail-sledge, pushed by the wind at an incredible speed.
At last, on 11 December, they arrived in New York. The steamer for Liverpool had left forty-five minutes before.
There was no other steamer for several days. Fogg went all round the port, and he found a small merchant ship, the Henrietta, that was leaving for Bordeaux.

The captain refused to change course. So Fogg paid for the journey to Bordeaux, went on board with his companions, and within a few hours he had persuaded the crew, with handfuls of banknotes, to obey him rather than their captain.
The captain was locked in his cabin, and the Henrietta set course for Liverpool.
But in the middle of the Atlantic, the engineer came to announce that there was no more coal.
Fogg then sent for the furious captain, and offered to buy his ship from him.
The captain accepted, on condition that he kept the hull and the engine. So Fogg gave an astonishing order: burn everything that was made of wood.
The cabins, the masts, the furniture, the deck itself disappeared one by one into the boiler.
When the Henrietta reached Ireland, it was nothing more than an iron hull. But it had lasted to the end.
On 21 December, at twenty to twelve, Phileas Fogg at last set foot on the quay at Liverpool. He was six hours from London.
It was then that Fix came up to him, put his hand on his shoulder, and said: 'Phileas Fogg, in the name of the Queen, I arrest you.'
Fogg was locked up in the customs house. He sat down on a bench, took out his watch, placed it on the table, and waited without saying a word.
At two thirty-three, the door opened. Fix came running in, his hair in disorder, unable to speak.
'Sir,' he stammered, 'forgive me... an unfortunate resemblance... The real thief was arrested three days ago... You are free!'
Phileas Fogg stood up, walked towards him, and, for perhaps the only time in his life, made a rapid movement: he punched him.
Then he hired a special train to London. But he had lost too much time.
When he arrived at the station, all the clocks in London said ten to nine.
He had gone round the world, and he was five minutes late. He had lost.
The next day, Fogg stayed shut up at home, calm as ever. He had almost nothing left of his fortune.
In the evening, he asked Aouda's forgiveness: he had brought her to England to keep her safe, and now he was ruined.
Aouda looked at him for a long time, then she took his hand. 'Mr Fogg, will you have me as your wife?'
For the first time, Phileas Fogg was moved. 'I love you,' he said simply.
Passepartout was sent to the priest to announce the wedding for the next day, Monday.
Ten minutes later, he came running back, his hair in disorder, unable to speak.
'My master... the wedding... impossible tomorrow... because tomorrow is Sunday! Today is Saturday!'
By travelling east, towards the sun, Fogg had seen the sun rise a little earlier every day.
Those few minutes gained every day had eventually added up to twenty-four hours: without knowing it, he had gained a whole day.
It was eight thirty-five. Fogg jumped into a carriage, crossed London at full speed, and at eight forty-four and fifty-seven seconds, he walked into the drawing room of the Reform Club.
Phileas Fogg had won his bet. But what had he really gained from this journey?
Nothing, people will say. Nothing indeed, except a charming wife, who made him the happiest of men.
Truly, wouldn't one go round the world for much less than that?

abri: shelter (mettre à l'abri = to keep safe)
arrêter: to stop (s'arrêter à = to stop at)
au: to the, at the, in the
au-devant: towards (au-devant du soleil = towards the sun)
avait-il: had he (peut-être avait-il trouvé = perhaps he had found)
cap: course (mettre le cap sur = to set course for)
carte: map (la carte du monde = the map of the world)
cartes: cards (jouer aux cartes = to play cards)
chez: at the home of (chez eux = at their place)
comme: like, as; how (comme c'est… ! = how … it is!)
coups: blows (à coups de billets = with handfuls of banknotes)
côtés: sides (de tous les côtés = on every side)
dire: to say (il faut dire = it must be said)
engager: to hire (se faire engager = to get hired)
entier: whole (le monde entier = the whole world)
fallait: was necessary (il fallait que = had to)
fallut: was necessary (il fallut = they had to)
façon: way (de la même façon = in the same way)
ferai: will do (je ferai le tour = I will go round)
ferait-on: would one (ne ferait-on pas = wouldn't one)
fit: made (le fit boire = made him drink); did
horloge: clock (réglée comme une horloge = like clockwork)
levait: raised (lever les yeux = to look up)
longs-nez: Long Noses (name of the acrobat troupe)
maison: home, house (à la maison = at home)
manquait: was missing (il manquait = there were … missing)
maître: master (maître de moi = my own master)
mit: put (mit le cap sur = set course for)
nouveau: new (quelque chose de nouveau = something new)
ordre: order (mettre en ordre = to sort out)
par: by, on (par terre = on the ground)
pied: foot (poser le pied = to set foot)
place: place (à sa place = in its place)
plein: full (en plein soleil = in broad sunlight)
plus: more; no longer (ne … plus); most (le plus)
rang: row (au premier rang = in the front row)
restait: remained, was left (il en restait = there were … left)
rire: to laugh; laughter (éclater de rire = to burst out laughing)
risque: risk (au risque de = at the risk of)
route: course (changer de route = to change course)
réglée: regulated (réglée comme une horloge = like clockwork)
sauta: jumped (sauter au cou de = to throw your arms round)
savile: Savile (Savile Row, a street in London)
sens: direction (dans tous les sens = in all directions)
seule: alone; only (la seule = the only one)
soient: have (qu'ils soient passés = for them to have passed)
suffisait: was enough (il lui suffisait de = all she had to do was)
tour: tour, trip around (faire le tour du monde = to go round the world)
trentaine: about thirty (une trentaine d'années = about thirty years old)
voulez-vous: will you (voulez-vous de moi = will you have me)
échoue: fails (pour que tout échoue = for everything to fail)
éclatèrent: burst (éclater de rire = to burst out laughing)
